notes.text: For 7 or 8, the pan is very full. Fry the rice in two batches, and stir half the egg, chicken, and sauce into each.

callback.body: You've diced before: planks, then sticks, then cubes. Today you'll dice chicken small, so every piece cooks through in the few minutes a stir-fry takes.

move.title: Hot pan, fast hands
move.body: Stir-frying means cooking small pieces in a very hot pan, keeping them moving, for just a few minutes. Today you'll make fried rice: scrambled egg, diced chicken, vegetables, and rice cooked the day before, tossed with soy sauce. Have everything ready before the stove goes on, because once it starts, it goes fast.

why.title: Why yesterday's rice
why.body: Fresh rice is warm, soft, and full of steam. In a hot pan it clumps and turns mushy. A night in the fridge dries the outside of each grain and firms it up, so the grains stay separate and fry instead of steaming.

why.title: Everything ready first
why.body: A stir-fry is over in about 10 minutes. There's no time to chop an onion while the rice is in the pan. Cut, measure, and line everything up next to the stove before you turn it on.

why.title: Small pieces, high heat
why.body: Small pieces cook all the way through in minutes, and high heat browns their outsides fast. Big pieces would burn outside before the middle cooked. That's why stir-fry is all about small, even cuts.

why.title: Spread, wait, toss
why.body: Rice only toasts while it's touching the hot pan. Spread it flat, leave it for a minute so it can crisp a little, then toss and spread again. Constant stirring keeps it from ever browning.

wrong.sign: The rice is mushy and clumpy
wrong.fix: The rice was too fresh or too wet. Spread it flat and let it sit longer between tosses. Next time, cook it the day before, or spread fresh rice on a sheet pan in the fridge for an hour.

wrong.sign: Everything is sticking to the pan
wrong.fix: Add a little more oil around the edges and scrape with the spatula. Wait for the pan to get hot again before adding more.
Add soy sauce a teaspoon at a time and a pinch of salt, tossing and tasting until you like it.
Keep stirring it in the hot pan for another minute or two, then check again.

quiz.q: Why use rice that was cooked the day before?
choices: It's drier, so the grains fry instead of clumping
quiz.explain: Chilled rice firms up and dries, so each grain stays separate in the pan.

quiz.q: When should you chop the green onions?
quiz.explain: A stir-fry moves fast. Everything needs to be ready before you start.

ingredients.prep: uncooked amount: cook it the day before and chill it

steps.text: Take the cold rice out of the fridge. Break up the clumps with your fingers until the grains are loose.
Slice the green onions into thin rings, keeping the white parts and the green parts in two piles. Peel and mince the garlic. Measure out the frozen peas and carrots.
steps.tip: Line everything up next to the stove in the order it goes in.

steps.text: Dice the chicken into small cubes, about ½ inch. Put them in the small bowl and sprinkle with {qty:salt} salt and the pepper.
steps.tip: Cut planks, then sticks, then cubes, just like vegetables.

steps.text: Wash your hands, the knife, and the cutting board with hot, soapy water.
steps.tip: Raw chicken can carry germs. Wash before you touch anything else.

steps.text: Crack the {n:egg} eggs into the medium bowl and beat them with the fork until smooth.
Wash your hands with soap, and wipe the counter where the eggs were.
Heat a third of the oil in the skillet over medium-high heat until it shimmers. Pour in the eggs and stir gently with the spatula until they're set in soft pieces. Slide them onto the plate.
Look closely at the eggs on the plate.

target.look: No wet, shiny, runny egg left anywhere.

steps.tip: If any part is still runny, slide it back in the pan for a few seconds.

steps.text: Add another third of the oil to the pan and turn the heat up to high. Tip the chicken in from the bowl and spread it out.
steps.tip: Tip it in close to the pan, away from you, so the oil doesn't splash.

steps.text: Wash your hands with soap, and wash the bowl the chicken was in.
Cook the chicken, stirring every 30 seconds or so, until it's white all over and browned in spots.
Slide the thermometer into the biggest piece of chicken. It needs to read at least 165°F. If it doesn't, cook 1 more minute and check again.
Add the white parts of the green onions, the garlic, and the peas and carrots. Stir-fry until the peas are bright green and hot.

Push everything to the sides, add the rest of the oil in the middle, and add the rice. Spread it flat and leave it for a minute, then toss everything together and spread it flat again. Keep going until the rice is hot and a little toasty.
steps.look: The grains are separate and hot, and some are golden and crisp.

steps.text: Pour the soy sauce around the edge of the pan so it sizzles, then add the sesame oil, the eggs, and the green parts of the onions. Toss for a minute until everything is mixed and the eggs are hot again.
steps.tip: Soy sauce poured around the hot edge sizzles and toasts. Poured in the middle, it just makes one soggy spot.

steps.text: Turn off the stove. Taste a spoonful, after letting it cool, and add a splash more soy sauce if it needs it. Serve hot.

vegetables.text: Slice the green onions into thin rings, keeping the white parts and the green parts in two piles. Measure out the jarred garlic and the frozen peas and carrots.
vegetables.tip: Line everything up next to the stove in the order it goes in.

dice-chicken.text: A grown-up dices the chicken into small cubes, about ½ inch, and puts them in the small bowl. Sprinkle them with {qty:salt} salt and the pepper.
dice-chicken.tip: Watch how the chicken is cut: planks, then sticks, then cubes. You'll cut raw chicken yourself later in the course.
